questions.question: A homeless man is admitted to hospital with fever. Blood and urine cultures are negative. Blood film shows tiny thin coiled organisms.
questions.question_raw: A homeless man is admitted to hospital with fever. Blood and urine cultures negative. Blood film shows tiny thin coiled organisms.

parts.text: What are 2 vectors for this organism?

parts_raw.text: What are 2 vectors for this organism?

questions.model_answer: a) Borrelia recurrentis, the spirochete causing louse-borne relapsing fever (LBRF) — the clinical setting of a homeless/crowded-living patient with fever and spirochetes on blood smear points to LBRF; the broader genus cause is relapsing fever Borrelia species. b) Two recognized vectors of relapsing fever Borrelia: (1) the body louse Pediculus humanus (vector of B. recurrentis/LBRF); (2) soft-bodied Ornithodoros ticks (e.g., O. hermsi) which transmit tick-borne relapsing fever.

questions.question: A hunter from wilderness in Washington State presents with relapsing fever.
questions.question_raw: PM Q4. A hunter from wilderness in Washington State with relapsing fever

parts.text: What is the syndrome and cause?
How will you diagnose the illness?
What is the pathogenesis of the relapsing fever?

parts_raw.text: a) What is the syndrome and cause?
b) How will you diagnose the illness?
d) What is the pathogenesis of the relapsing fever?

questions.model_answer: a) Tick-borne relapsing fever (TBRF), caused by Borrelia hermsii, transmitted by the soft tick Ornithodoros hermsi in the western United States/Canada (exposure to rodent-infested cabins/woodpiles). b) Identify spirochetes on a Giemsa or Wright (or acridine orange) stained blood smear drawn during a febrile episode (~70% sensitive in TBRF; negative smears do not exclude it). If smear negative: acute/convalescent serology (IFA/ELISA), PCR, and confirmation by mouse inoculation or culture in modified Kelly medium. c) Doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily (or tetracycline 500 mg qid, or erythromycin 500 mg qid if tetracyclines contraindicated) for 7-10 days; CNS involvement requires parenteral penicillin G or ceftriaxone for 14 days. Observe for a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction after the first dose. d) Relapses are due to antigenic variation of the spirochete's variable major protein (vmp): during fever, organisms divide rapidly and are visible on smear; a specific antibody response to the dominant vmp clears them (afebrile period), but the spirochete then expresses a different vmp (via recombination of vmp genes on linear plasmids), producing recurrent spirochetemia and fever, and the cycle repeats.

cohort_answer.text:
Tick-borne Relapsing fever (TBRF) caused by borrelia spirochetes: B hermsii (Northwest NA), B turicatae (Southwest/South Central), B. miyamotoi, B parkerii. (Louse-borne RF caused by B recurrentis). Symptoms: episodic fever after 7 days incubation, lasts 3 days, separated by 7 afebrile days, H/A, arthralgias, myalgias, N/V, abdominal pain. Rarely ARDS, liver impairment, encephalopathy. Tick: Ornithodorus hermsi/turicatae; Louse: Pediculus humanus
Spirochetemia with microscopy (Giemsa or Wright stains); if not seen: PCR (also on CSF); Blood culture on BSK media; inoculation in immature mice; Serology for confirmation with 4-fold titer increase
TBRF Mild: Doxycycline 100mg PO BID x7-10 days (or erythromycin 500mg q6h x7-10 days). If CNS: Ceftriaxone 2g or Penicillin G x10-14 days. Risk of Jarisch Herxheimer reaction (50%) managed with cooling blankets/antipyretics. LBRF: Tetracycline 500mg PO x1 dose
Febrile episodes correlate with high spirochetemia (>10^5-10^6) with immune recognition, subsequently sequestered in internal organs where spirochete undergoes antigenic variation of outer surface proteins, evading immune system, causing new febrile episode

questions.question: A person camping in Washington State returns with recurrent fever.
questions.question_raw: Q67 (2015). Person camping in Washington State, returns with recurrent fever.

parts.text: How to make a quick diagnosis?
The patient develops hypotension and fever after receiving treatment — what is the cause of this?

parts_raw.text: B) Why is there recurrent fever?
C) How to make a quick diagnosis?
E) Patient develops hypotension/fever after receiving tx - what is the cause of this?

questions.model_answer: a) Tick-borne relapsing fever (TBRF). b) Antigenic variation: the spirochete periodically switches its variable major protein (vmp); antibody clears the dominant serotype (afebrile interval), then a new vmp is expressed, causing recurrent spirochetemia and fever. c) Examine a Giemsa- or Wright-stained (thick and thin) peripheral blood smear drawn during a febrile episode for spirochetes (~70% sensitive in TBRF); PCR of blood is an alternative. d) Borrelia hermsii (transmitted by Ornithodoros hermsi in the western US). e) Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction — rigors, fever, leukopenia, and hypotension occurring in about half of patients, usually within ~2 hours of the first antibiotic dose (can be later), from rapid spirochete killing.

cohort_answer.text: A) Tick borne relapsing fever. B) Due to multiphasic antigenic variation - reappearance of spirochetes in blood with relapses. C) Blood thick and thin smear (look for spirochetes); PCR from blood. D) Borrelia hermsii (mountainous West). E) Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, typically within 4h of initiating abx.
